safety.title: Safety
safety.accessibilityToggleLabel: If this is hard for you to do

familyPlan.title: Make a family plan
familyPlan.body1: Agree on a meeting point outside your home and another outside your neighborhood, in case you cannot reach each other by phone right after a strong earthquake. Make sure every family member — including children and grandparents — knows both points and how to get there on foot.
familyPlan.body2: Keep a paper list of important phone numbers (family, neighbors, doctor) somewhere everyone can find it. Phone networks are often overloaded for hours after a strong earthquake, so do not rely on your phone alone.

secureHome.title: Secure your home
secureHome.body1: Anchor tall or heavy furniture — wardrobes, bookshelves, wall units — to the wall so it cannot tip over. Move heavy objects to lower shelves, and keep beds and sofas away from tall unsecured furniture.
secureHome.body2: Two hazards common in Kurdish homes deserve special attention: rooftop water tanks should be checked and secured by whoever installed them, and gas cylinders should always stand upright, be strapped or braced so they cannot fall or roll, and be kept away from any flame or heat source.

emergencyKit.title: Prepare an emergency kit
emergencyKit.body1: Keep a bag ready with drinking water, a few days of any medicine your family needs, copies of important documents (ID cards, property papers), a torch and spare batteries, a portable phone charger, and some cash — card machines and the internet may not work for a while after a strong earthquake.
emergencyKit.body2: Store the kit somewhere you can grab it quickly, and check it every few months so the water stays fresh and the medicine has not expired.

safeSpots.title: Know the safe spot in every room
safeSpots.body1: In each room you spend time in, pick a safe spot in advance: under a sturdy table or desk, or against an interior wall away from windows, mirrors, and tall furniture. Avoid exterior walls, which are more likely to be damaged.
safeSpots.body2: Doorways are not safer in modern buildings — that is an old idea that no longer matches how buildings are built today. A sturdy table gives you real protection from falling objects; an open doorway does not.

schoolWork.title: Know the plan at school and work
schoolWork.body1: Ask your children's school and your workplace what their earthquake plan is: where to shelter during shaking, and where to gather afterward. Encourage schools and offices to practice a Drop-Cover-Hold On drill, not just a fire drill.
schoolWork.body2: If you manage a classroom, office, or shop, walk through the space and note the safe spots and nearest exits, so you can guide others calmly if shaking starts while people are with you.

dropCoverHold.title: Drop, Cover, and Hold On
dropCoverHold.body1: The moment you feel shaking: drop to your hands and knees before it knocks you down, take cover under a sturdy table or desk, and hold on to it, ready to move with it if it shifts. If no table is nearby, cover your head and neck with your arms.
dropCoverHold.body2: Stay there until the shaking fully stops. Most earthquake injuries come from falling or from objects falling, not from buildings collapsing — protecting your head and neck for those seconds is the single most effective thing you can do.

protectHeadNeckVsDoorway.do: Get low, take cover under something sturdy, and hold on.
protectHeadNeckVsDoorway.dont: Do not run to a doorway — a modern doorway is no stronger than the rest of the room and gives you no real protection.

wheelchair.label: If you use a wheelchair
wheelchair.body: Lock your wheelchair's wheels, stay seated, lean forward over your lap, and cover your head and neck with your arms or anything soft nearby. If you can safely move away from windows or unsecured furniture first, do so — otherwise stay where you are.

caneOrWalker.label: If you use a cane or walker
caneOrWalker.body: Sit down on the nearest sturdy chair, bed, or bench and stay seated. Cover your head and neck with your arms. Keep your cane or walker close, but do not stand up to reach for it while the ground is still shaking.

bed.label: If you are in bed
bed.body: Stay in bed. Roll onto your stomach if you can, and cover your head and neck with a pillow. Do not get up to find cover elsewhere — most injuries in this situation come from falling while trying to move in the dark.

indoors.title: If you are indoors when shaking starts
indoors.body1: Stay inside. Move only the few steps needed to reach your nearest safe spot, then Drop, Cover, and Hold On. Exits are usually more dangerous during shaking than staying put — glass, signs, and building parts can fall right outside doors.

stayInVsRunOutside.do: Shelter where you are and wait for the shaking to stop.
stayInVsRunOutside.dont: Do not run outside while the ground is still shaking — most injuries happen while people are moving.

outdoors.title: If you are outdoors when shaking starts
outdoors.body1: Move to open ground, away from buildings, walls, trees, and power lines, and Drop, Cover, and Hold On there. The area right next to a building is one of the most dangerous places to be — that is where falling glass, tiles, and cladding land.

openGroundVsBuildings.do: Get clear of buildings and power lines, then get low and cover your head.
openGroundVsBuildings.dont: Do not stand close to a building, wall, or power line — even one that looks undamaged.

vehicle.title: If you are in a vehicle
vehicle.body1: Pull over as soon as you safely can, away from bridges, overpasses, tunnels, and power lines, and stay inside the vehicle with your seatbelt on until the shaking stops. A car gives you real protection from falling debris.

pullOverVsOverpass.do: Pull over to a clear spot and stay in your seat with the seatbelt on.
pullOverVsOverpass.dont: Do not stop on or under a bridge, overpass, or tunnel.

commonMyths.title: Two habits worth unlearning
commonMyths.body1: These two habits feel protective but current guidance advises against them — knowing this in advance means you will not lose time to them when it matters.

headNeckVsDoorwayMyth.do: Cover your head and neck under something sturdy.
headNeckVsDoorwayMyth.dont: Do not treat a doorway as a safe spot — that guidance is outdated.

stairsVsElevator.do: Once shaking stops, leave a damaged building calmly by the stairs.
stairsVsElevator.dont: Do not use the elevator — power and elevator shafts are often affected by a strong earthquake.

aftershocks.title: Expect aftershocks
aftershocks.body1: Smaller earthquakes — aftershocks — often follow a strong one, sometimes for days or weeks. Each time you feel shaking, Drop, Cover, and Hold On again; a smaller aftershock does not mean it is safe to stop taking shaking seriously.
aftershocks.body2: If you felt the earthquake, you can report what you experienced in this app's felt-report screen — it takes under a minute and helps build a real record of shaking across Kurdistan, town by town.

checkHazards.title: Check for injuries and hazards
checkHazards.body1: Check yourself and the people around you for injuries first, and give first aid if you can. Then check for hazards: a gas smell, damaged wiring, or a leaning gas cylinder.

gasLeakSafety.do: If you smell gas, shut the cylinder or main valve, open windows, and leave the building.
gasLeakSafety.dont: Do not switch on lights, use a lighter, or strike a match if you smell gas.

evacuateCarefully.title: Leave a damaged building carefully
evacuateCarefully.body1: If your building looks damaged, leave calmly using the stairs, watching for broken glass, fallen objects, and cracked stairwells on the way.

reentryCaution.do: Leave and wait outside, at a safe distance from the building.
reentryCaution.dont: Do not go back inside until it has been checked and declared safe by someone qualified.

reliableInfo.title: Get information from reliable sources
reliableInfo.body1: After a strong earthquake, rumors spread quickly — about aftershock predictions, damage, or danger — faster than facts can be checked. Follow official sources (civil defense, geological authorities, this app) for confirmed information, and be patient with what is still unknown.

verifyBeforeSharing.do: Check information against an official source before you act on it or share it.
verifyBeforeSharing.dont: Do not forward earthquake predictions or damage claims you cannot verify — even from someone you trust.

helpNeighbors.title: Help others if you safely can
helpNeighbors.body1: Once you and your family are safe, check on elderly neighbors, people with disabilities, and anyone living alone nearby — a knock on the door and a few minutes can matter.

helpSafely.do: Check on neighbors who may need help, and call for emergency services if someone is seriously hurt.
helpSafely.dont: Do not move a seriously injured person yourself unless they are in immediate danger, such as fire — moving them incorrectly can make an injury worse.

mission.title: Always know, in your language
mission.description: Bumelerze brings fast, scientifically correct earthquake information to Kurdistan — in Sorani, Kurmanji, Arabic, and English. Built by earthquake researchers who work this region.

language.title: Choose your language
language.description: Pick the language Bumelerze should use. You can change this again anytime in Settings.

location.title: Your location makes science better
location.description: Sharing your location lets Bumelerze show accurate distances and turns your "did you feel it?" reports into valid scientific testimony that helps map real shaking. You can change this anytime in Settings.

notifications.title: Alerts are coming
notifications.description: Soon, Bumelerze will notify you the moment an earthquake happens near you or near a place you care about (your HomeBase). We'll ask for notification permission when that feature launches.

homeBase.title: Set your HomeBase
homeBase.description: If you live away from Kurdistan, pick a HomeBase town — like where your family lives — so future alerts can watch it for you too. Optional; you can set or change this later in Settings.

done.title: You're all set
done.description: Bumelerze is ready. You'll land on the live earthquake feed for your region every time you open the app.

situation.title: Where were you during the earthquake?

othersFelt.title: Did other people near you feel it?

options.some: Some felt it, most did not
options.everyone: Everyone or almost everyone felt it

motion.title: How would you describe the shaking?

stand.title: Was it difficult to stand or walk?

options.fell: Yes, I fell or was thrown to the ground

shelf.title: Did objects rattle, topple over, or fall off shelves?

options.few_fell: A few items toppled or fell

picture.title: Did pictures on the wall move or get knocked crooked?

furniture.title: Did furniture or heavy appliances slide, topple, or move?

buildingDamageLevel.title: Was the building you were in damaged?

options.1: Small cracks — hairline cracks in plaster or walls, a few fallen plaster pieces
options.2: Serious damage — large wall cracks, fallen plaster chunks or masonry, broken windows, damaged parapet or roof tank
options.3: Partial or full collapse — walls or floors fell, building unusable

roadDamageLevel.title: Did you see damage to roads or the ground?

options.1: Small cracks in roads or ground
options.2: Large cracks; broken water or sewage pipes
options.3: Landslide, collapsed road, or large ground failure
